analysis.one_liner: Bases seniors' Medicare drug coinsurance on the discounted price, not the inflated list price.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in July 2025, the bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Many Medicare drug plans charge seniors coinsurance as a percentage of a drug's list price — the sticker price drug companies set high, even though insurers pay much less after manufacturer discounts. Seniors end up paying a percentage of the inflated number instead of the real one. This bill would require that coinsurance be figured on the lower net price whenever the net price is lower, cutting seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees whose prescriptions carry coinsurance instead of a flat copay. Whenever the plan's actual (net) cost of the drug is below the list price, their coinsurance would be calculated on the lower net price, so they pay less out of pocket.

how_it_helps.text: Requires coinsurance for Part D drugs in the initial coverage phase to be calculated on the drug's net price — the negotiated price net of manufacturer concessions — rather than the list price, whenever net price is lower [S2] [S3].
Defines net price using the manufacturer price concessions already reported by plan sponsors in the Detailed DIR Report, so the discount data already exists to implement it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit intermediaries would collect less coinsurance from enrollees, since their revenue was tied to the higher list price; they could shift some of that to premiums. Brand-name drug makers would face more visible gaps between list prices and actual prices, and could face more pressure to lower list prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not force manufacturers to lower list prices or disclose discounts publicly; it only moves seniors' cost-sharing onto the discounted figure, leaving the underlying high list prices in place [S3].
Plans that lose coinsurance revenue could offset it by raising premiums or other cost-sharing, spreading the cost to enrollees who use less expensive drugs [S3].

The change applies only to costs above the deductible and below the annual out-of-pocket threshold, and it excludes certain drugs already covered by other negotiated-pricing rules, so not every senior or every drug benefits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: seniors who pay percentage coinsurance on drugs with big list-versus-net gaps would see lower bills, and the mechanism uses discount data that plans already report. The costs are modest and mostly absorbed by plans and drugmakers' pricing optics, but the bill is narrow — it does nothing to lower the sticker prices themselves and leaves most Part D cost-sharing arrangements untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Sen. Jacky Rosen introduced the bill on July 31, 2025, with Sen. John Cornyn as an original cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
The bill remains in the Finance Committee with no further action listed in its history, and the 119th Congress is still in session [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Part D plans and pharmacy benefit intermediaries are better off so far, since the requirement lowering seniors' coinsurance has not advanced and their cost-sharing collections tied to list prices continue unchanged.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making it bipartisan on day one

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since July 2025

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor introduced it with one of 55 Senate Republicans as an original cosponsor; no opposition has been recorded because no vote has occurred.

industries.industry: Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit intermediaries
industries.note: Plans currently collect coinsurance calculated on the higher list price even though they pay the lower net price after manufacturer concessions; this bill cuts that spread out of seniors' bills. They could raise premiums to compensate. [S3] [S2]

Drugmakers keep charging high list prices while offering concessions to plans; under this bill those high list prices could no longer be passed through to seniors as inflated coinsurance. Manufacturers lose some pricing cover but owe the same concessions as before. [S2] [S3]

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no scheduled action and only a bipartisan pair of senators behind it. Bills like this usually advance only if attached to a larger Medicare or drug-pricing package before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027; on its own, it is likely to die in committee at the end of the session.
